To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

inhibition of p38α causes an acute energy deficit in cancer cells and triggers autophagy as an adaptive response to restore energy levels; the autophagy response is linked to AMPK-Foxo3a axis, which is activated in a cancer-specific metabolic context
inhibition of p38α in CRCs leads to a rapid drop in energy levels, which triggers AMPK-dependent FoxO3A activation, autophagy, and cell death.

1) p38α inhibition causes an acute drop in ATP levels, which triggers AMPK-dependent activation of autophagy and cell cycle arrest; 2) autophagy is required to sustain cell cycle arrest, and its inhibition leads to cell death; and 3) p38α blockade has a cytostatic effect in vivo.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of novel therapeutic approaches to target cancer metabolism and autophagy.
the identification of novel molecular targets that may represent potential therapeutic strategies for CRC treatment.
identifying the molecular mechanisms that underlie the link between autophagy and cancer metabolism, and the potential therapeutic implications of these findings.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
autophagy is a survival response to metabolic stress, but that it may become a death response if the stress is not resolved.
autophagy in CRCs can either be an adaptive or a cytotoxic process, depending on the metabolic status.
p38α blockade in cancer cells triggers autophagy and a switch in the metabolic state, which is associated with cell cycle arrest and death.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
p38α inhibition unveils a novel axis linking autophagic and metabolic pathways to the control of cancer cell fate.
p38α inhibition in cancer cells causes a metabolic crisis that is resolved by autophagy and that, in case of persistence of the stress, leads to cell cycle arrest and death.
the inhibition of p38α induces a metabolic crisis, which is sensed by the AMPK-FoxOs axis and triggers autophagy, leading to the death of cancer cells.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the p38α-FoxO3 pathway may represent an attractive target to treat cancers with low glycolytic activity, such as colorectal, pancreatic or hepatocellular cancers, as well as other types of cancer that rely on alternative metabolic pathways.
the p38α-AMPK-FoxO pathway is a potential therapeutic target in CRC, as its inhibition causes cell cycle arrest and death of cancer cells with a low glycolytic activity.

the inhibition of p38α, an established drug target, may represent a novel therapeutic approach in CRC, which could be used in combination with other drugs, such as inhibitors of the mTORC1 complex or HIF1α.
